paras: The Grand Haven jail lynching attempt was a march by several hundred farmers on the Ottawa County jail at Grand Haven, Michigan, on the night of May 14, 1881, to take out and hang Albertus Voskamp, a hired man accused of murdering his employer. Militia ordered out by the governor met the crowd at the jail, and after a parley it went home without violence, warning that it would return if Voskamp were not convicted. Voskamp, described as a Prussian or German, was later convicted and sentenced to life.

On May 9, 1881, Lyman H. Cady, a young farmer near Lamont in Ottawa County, was shot dead on his farm, and his hired man of about three weeks was arrested. According to the Chicago Tribune's Grand Haven correspondent, the two had quarreled over wages, and the prisoner said he had acted in self-defense. Before the train left with the prisoner, a crowd of Cady's neighbors tried to lynch him and at one point had a rope around his neck, but Sheriff Vaupell got him aboard and lodged him in the Grand Haven jail.

On May 14 the Tribune reported "great excitement" in Grand Haven over word that an organized body of about 200 men was coming to take Voskamp from jail and hang him. The sheriff, forewarned of meetings held for that purpose, garrisoned the jail with armed officers and asked Gov. Jerome to call out Company F of the Second Regiment of state troops. The governor's order arrived, and some forty militiamen, armed and in uniform, formed in the jail yard.

The crowd, put at about 250 by the Tribune's May 15 special and at 300 by the wire, came down from around Berlin, Lamont and Allendale on a river boat, landed at Bailey's Mill and marched silently into the city at about 11:30 p.m. Prosecuting Attorney McBride stopped them at the gate, spoke to them, and invited two of their number ("a few" in the wire) to inspect the defenses inside. Satisfied that they could not take the prisoner without much bloodshed, the men left at 1 a.m., or 2 a.m. in the wire version. On leaving, they gave notice that they would lynch Voskamp, or come again "prepared for war", if he were not convicted.

Voskamp's trial, moved to Kalamazoo, ended on December 13, 1881, with a murder conviction after an insanity defense, and he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Six men charged with an attempt to lynch him were tried in November, but the jury failed to agree, and in February 1882 Judge Arnold of Grand Haven fined five named "would be lynchers of Voskamp" $100 each. Neither item says whether the charges concerned the May march on the jail or another attempt on the prisoner.

The episode was covered only in the white press. The Chicago Tribune carried two Grand Haven specials, the first headed "Threatened Lynching" and the second "Didn't Get Their Man", which closed by remarking that the farmers probably got home in time to do their Sunday chores. Both called Voskamp "the murderer" before any trial, and the first named the dead man "Hiram H. Coady".

The wire version ran in the Omaha Bee's "Record of Crime" column under "Meditated Lynching", describing the crowd as "a sober and orderly crowd". It was reprinted in Canton, Ohio, as "The Lynching of a Murderer Prevented" and condensed into a news brief in Liberty, Mississippi, two weeks after the event. None of the reports mentions race; the prisoner was identified only as a Prussian or German.

The size of the crowd was given as about 200 in the advance report, about 250 in the Tribune's detailed local special, and 300 in the wire. The local special, written closest to the event, also gives the earlier departure time and the smaller number of men allowed inside.

bases: A crowd of 250-300 men marched on the Grand Haven jail to take Voskamp out and hang him and was turned back by militia [A4, A5].
No one was killed: the crowd of 250-300 came to hang an accused murderer but withdrew when it found militia guarding the jail [A4, A5]; it is an attempted lynching.
Two separate Chicago Tribune local specials and an independent wire account agree on the march, the militia and the withdrawal [A3, A4, A5].

accounts.label: Grand Haven special, May 14 (Chicago Tribune)
accounts.gist: Reported great excitement over an organized body of about 200 men said to be coming to take Voskamp from jail and hang him, and the sheriff's preparations to fight.

accounts.label: Grand Haven special, May 15 (Chicago Tribune)
accounts.gist: About 250 farmers came down the river by boat, marched silently into the city, were stopped at the jail gate by 40 militiamen and the prosecutor, sent two men to inspect the defenses, and left quietly at 1 a.m.

accounts.label: Wire report (Omaha Bee, Stark County Democrat, Southern Herald)
accounts.gist: Three hundred men appeared about midnight, found militia before the jail, heard District Attorney McBride, sent 'a few' inside, and left at 2 a.m., warning they would lynch him (or return 'prepared for war') if he were not convicted.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune ran local specials under 'Threatened Lynching' and 'Didn't Get Their Man', calling Voskamp 'the murderer' and noting the farmers would get home in time 'to do their farm chores'.

The Omaha Bee printed the wire in a 'Record of Crime' column under 'Meditated Lynching' and called the crowd 'sober and orderly'; Ohio and Mississippi papers reprinted it as 'The Lynching of a Murderer Prevented' and a news brief.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of the prisoner's first and last name.
The May 14 Tribune dispatch and its Omaha reprint name the dead man 'Hiram H. Coady'; the earlier and later reports, including the Tribune's own of May 10 and 16, say Lyman H. Cady.
The 200 figure was a forecast; the 250 comes from the more detailed local special of May 15.
